sets.title: The mushroom book
sets.transcript:

sets.title: Two hens in the garden
sets.transcript:
M: So, Effie, your mum says you've got a plan, and that I'm the one to ask.
W: Yeah, Uncle Eamon, because you kept hens for years. I want to keep two of them in our back garden.
M: Hens? Last summer it was a rabbit, and that lasted about a week.
W: This is different. We throw away so much food, and hens eat things like vegetable peel and old rice. Plus, eggs. I've worked it all out. Two hens lay about ten eggs a week, and we only eat about six.
M: And the other four?
W: Elsie next door wants to buy them. She's already asked me twice when I'm getting the hens.
M: Okay, you've thought about the eggs. Now the hard part. Hens have to be shut in their house before dark, every single night, or a fox gets them. I lost three that way.
W: Wait, there are foxes around here? I didn't know they came into gardens.
M: Oh, they do. I saw one by the bins last week. And you're away at camp for three weeks in July. Who's shutting the door then?
W: Mum could do it.
M: Your mum's on night shifts all summer, and you know what my sister's like when she's tired. Honestly, I'd wait until next spring, after camp, when you've read up on it properly.
W: Next spring? That's ages away. And I have read up on it. I know how much space they need and everything.
M: Fair enough. But space is one thing, and foxes are another. They're clever, and they're hungry.
W: So what would make you say yes?
M: Someone who's home every evening while you're at camp. Ask Elsie if she'd do it. If she says yes, I'll come round and check your fence, and we'll decide later. I'm not saying yes or no today.
W: Okay. I'll ask her tonight. I'm already thinking of names, though.

speakers.S: a teacher giving a short lecture to a high-school class

sets.title: Bottled food before germs
sets.transcript:
So today I want to talk about something that's sitting in almost every kitchen cupboard: food sealed in a can or a jar. Most people assume this was invented in a laboratory, that scientists first worked out what makes food go bad and then designed a way to stop it. It's a nice, tidy story. It's also backwards, and the way it really happened tells us something about how discoveries get made.

Let's go back to France in the seventeen nineties. The country was at war, and its soldiers and sailors had a serious problem. Fresh food rotted long before it could be eaten. Salted meat and hard biscuits lasted, but people got sick living on them for months. So the government offered a large cash prize to anyone who could find a better way to keep food.

The person who solved it wasn't a scientist at all. His name was Nicolas Appert, and he was a sweet maker in Paris, someone who spent his days boiling sugar and fruit. Appert had no theory. What he had was patience. He packed food into thick glass bottles, the heavy kind used for wine, pushed the corks in tight, sealed them with wax, and then set the bottles in boiling water. Then he waited, opened them weeks or months later, and wrote down what he found.

Here's the interesting part. He kept this up for roughly fifteen years. Peas needed one heating time, meat needed another, fruit another. If he heated a bottle too briefly, the food spoiled. If a cork let in even a little air, the food spoiled. Bit by bit, food by food, he built up a set of rules that worked, without ever knowing why they worked. Around eighteen ten he won the prize, and part of the deal was that he had to publish everything in a book, so anyone could copy his method.

So did the scientists step in at this point and explain it? Some tried. One of the leading chemists in France examined the bottles and announced that the answer was air. Keep the air out, he said, and food can't decay. It sounded convincing, and for a long time nobody could show otherwise.

It was wrong. About fifty years later, Louis Pasteur showed that food spoils because of microbes, living things far too small to see, which drift through the air and multiply in food. Appert's boiling killed the microbes already inside the bottle, and his tight seal stopped new ones from getting in. Air on its own, without the microbes, didn't make the food rot. So the explanation came half a century after the method, and the first scientific explanation pointed at the wrong thing.

So when someone tells you that understanding always comes first and useful inventions follow, I'd say be careful. Appert didn't need the theory. He needed careful notes and the stubbornness to open bottle after bottle of spoiled peas. Honestly, I find that more impressive than a lucky flash of insight, because there was no flash. There were just years of small tests.

For next class, think of one other everyday thing that people used successfully long before anyone could explain it.
